newsitem.title: USA: NOW targets Smith Barney as 'merchant of shame'.
newsitem.headline: NOW targets Smith Barney as 'merchant of shame'.

text.p: The National Organisation for Women on Wednesday targeted the brokerage house Smith Barney as a "merchant of shame" for alleged incidents of sexual harassment and discrimination against women.
"Many businesses are 'doing business the old-fashioned way,' as Smith Barney's slogan puts it -- they're still exploiting women," NOW president Patricia Ireland said in a statement.
Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive officer of Smith Barney, strongly disagreed with NOW's statement.

"I think what NOW has done is both unsubstantiated and reckless," Dimon said by telephone from New York. "... I think we have some of the most ambitious programmes to promote fairness in the workplace ... I totally dispute their contention and I think it's disgraceful."

Ireland said NOW was singling out Smith Barney "because this company's bad practices are common practices." NOW planned to take action against the brokerage house through "direct action and consumer pressure campaigns," she said.

In a telephone interview with Reuters, Ireland said NOW chapters planned informational picketing outside Smith Barney branch offices "when we're ready," especially offices where alleged acts of sex harassment and discrimination occurred.
These include Garden City, N.Y., Richmond, Va., Knoxville, Tenn., Kansas City and Seattle, Ireland said, in addition to offices in New York City, Chicago, Atlanta and Miami.

Pickets will distribute fliers to customers "asking them to consider before investing with Smith Barney whether that's where they want their money to go, to invest with someone whose judgment is, to us, not very good," she said. "What we want to do is have an escalating campaign that gives them every opportunity to change their approach."

Twenty-six women have filed suit against Smith Barney, alleging sexual harassment and discrimination, and are seeking to certify the suit as a class action that could potentially involve hundreds of female employees, according to Linda Friedman, a Chicago attorney whose firm represents the women.

Friedman said the suit contends that Smith Barney steers women to lower-paying, more traditionally female, clerical jobs, while men become brokers, assistant branch managers and branch managers. It alleges that the few women who become brokers or branch managers do not receive the same administrative support that men do, such as having adequate staff for clerical chores, Friedman said in a telephone interview.
When the suit was filed last year, there were about 10 women branch managers among Smith Barney's 460 branches, she said.

The suit also maintains that women at Smith Barney have been called derogatory names and been subjected to physical assault. Friedman described some actions against women at Smith Barney as "disgusting, sophomoric discriminatory stuff -- pranks that are not funny but are offensive."
The suit alleges that women who complain about sexual harassment or sex discrimination are met with retaliation including demotions and firings.
